translations.text: The Life of Apa Aphou, the Hermit and Bishop of Oxyrhynchus. The twenty-first day of Thout.
After these things, we must remember the holy bishop.
His name among people was Aphou.

People also called him “the Strong One.” At first he had lived under the direction of chosen and faithful men, who themselves had met some of the apostles’ disciples. He conducted himself according to their dignified way of life.
After they fell asleep in death, he remained alone, knowing only one brother, who had also learned from them, together with him, the way to ascend to heaven.
Aphou was pleased to live this kind of life. He stripped off his clothes and tied a skin around his waist. He continued living with the gazelles in the desert, spending both day and night in worship.
His food was like that on which those animals lived.
Although he bore the body of human weakness, he made himself like them. For he had begun this kind of life as soon as he was weaned in childhood.
He would meet the brother we mentioned earlier once each year, and the brother would tell him the day of the holy proclamation.
He would come out wearing an ordinary layman’s robe and listen to the Easter proclamation in the church of Oxyrhynchus. No one would recognize him before he returned to his place.
He continued living this way until he began to grow old.

He was stronger than the animals with which he roamed. They recognized him as a companion and also loved him as a shepherd. They gave him great comfort, like rational human beings, as though holy providence had assigned them to him, because they saw the mark of their Lord upon him.
In winter they would gather around him, so that he became warm among them, like someone staying in a shelter, because of all their breath reaching him.
Likewise, in summer they would provide shade for him.

If one day he became ill and could not follow them when they went to eat, some would remain beside him, never leaving him alone. The others would go to graze and bring him in their mouths things he could eat. He acknowledged these things after he became bishop, because many of the brothers questioned him about this way of life, asking, “For what reason did you live this way?”
He told them these things: “For my part, I fall very far short.

Nevertheless, I heard blessed David say before God, ‘I became like the animals before you.’ I also heard about Isaiah, that he walked naked, and that even the sackcloth tied around his waist he was made to loosen. And concerning our Savior, the Lord of all, I read in the Gospel according to Mark that he was with the wild animals.
If God and his saints went through all these hardships for my sake, how much more should I, poor as I am!”
While he was still living with the wild animals, he happened to come out for the holy Easter proclamation.

He heard a statement that did not agree with the knowledge of the Holy Spirit, and he was deeply troubled by these words. Indeed, everyone who heard them was also saddened and troubled. But the angel of the Lord commanded blessed Aphou not to disregard the statement, telling him, “You have been appointed by the Lord to go to Alexandria and set this statement right.” The statement was of this kind: as though exalting the glory of God in his speech,
he recalled the weakness of human beings.

The man dictating said, “This is not the image of God that we human beings bear.” When blessed Aphou heard these things, he was filled with the Holy Spirit and traveled to the city of Alexandria, wearing a felt robe.
Blessed Apa Aphou stood at the door of the bishop’s residence for three days, and no one brought him inside to the bishop, because they regarded him as an ordinary man.
After this, one of the clergy took notice of him. He saw his perseverance and realized that he was a man of God.
He went inside and told the archbishop, “There is a poor man at the door who says, ‘I want to meet you.’”
“But we did not dare bring him in to you, because he is not wearing respectable clothing.” Immediately, as though moved by God, he ordered them to bring him in to him.
When he stood before him, he asked him his reason for coming.
He answered, “Let my lord the bishop listen to his servant’s words with love and patience.” He said to him, “Speak.”

The blessed Apa Aphou answered, “I know the goodness of your soul, that you are a man who accepts advice. That is why I have approached Your Eminence, confident that you will not despise a word of piety,
“even if it comes from a poor man such as me.”
Theophilus the archbishop said to him, “What godless person would be so foolish as to reject a word of God for any reason?”

Aphou answered, “Let my lord the bishop give orders for this passage in the copy of the sermon to be read to me, because I heard a statement in it that does not agree with the God-breathed Scriptures. I did not believe that it came from you, but I said, ‘Perhaps the scribes made a mistake while writing.’ Many devout people have taken offense at this and have become deeply distressed.”
Apa Theophilus the archbishop immediately gave an order, and they brought the copy of the sermon.

When they began reading and reached that statement, Apa Aphou immediately intervened, saying, “A statement like this is not correct. But I confess that all human beings were created in the image of God.”
The archbishop answered, “How is it that you alone have spoken about this statement, and no one else has spoken in support of you?”
Apa Aphou said, “But I am confident that you yourself will support me and will not oppose me.”
The archbishop said, “How can you say of an Ethiopian that he is the image of God,
“or of someone with leprosy, or a lame person, or a blind person?”
The blessed Apa Aphou answered, “If you say such things, you will be disputing with the one who said, ‘Let us make a human being according to our likeness and our image.’”
The archbishop answered, “May that never happen!
“But I think that Adam alone was created according to his likeness and his image, while the children he fathered after him do not resemble him.”

Apa Aphou answered, saying, “Yet after God established a covenant with Noah after the flood, he said to him, ‘Whoever sheds human blood, his own blood will be shed in return, because the human being was created in the image of God.’”

The archbishop said, “I am afraid to say that a sick, suffering person bears the image of God, who cannot suffer—a lowly person who sits outside and relieves himself. How can you think of him in connection with the true light, which nothing can stain?”
Aphou said to him, “If you say these things, people will also say of the body of Christ that we receive that it is not his body.
“For the Jews will say, ‘How can you take bread that the earth has produced and that is baked in an oven, and afterward believe in it, receiving it as the body of the Lord?’”
The archbishop said to him, “It is not like that. For it really is bread before we place it on the altar.

“When we place it on the altar and invoke God over them, the bread becomes the body of Christ, and the cup becomes blood, just as he said to his disciples, ‘Take and eat. This is my body and my blood.’ And again, not to believe [?].”
Apa Aphou said to him, “Just as it is necessary to believe this, it is necessary to believe in his authority, that the human being was created according to the likeness and image of God.
“For the one who said, ‘I am the bread that came from heaven,’
“is also the one who said, ‘Whoever sheds human blood, his own blood will be shed in return, because the human being was created in the image of God.’”

But concerning the glory of God’s greatness, which no one can see because of his unapproachable light, and concerning the weakness of humanity’s lowly condition, according to the natural limitations we know—
We think of it this way: it is like a king ordering a portrait to be painted, and everyone acknowledging, “This is the king’s portrait.”
“At the same time, they all know that it is wood and medicines.”
For its nose is not prominent like a human being’s.
Nor are its ears like those on the king’s face.
Nor does it speak as he does.
And no one thinks about all these deficiencies in it, because they fear the king’s declaration, since he said, “This is my portrait.”

Indeed, if someone dares to deny it, saying, “This is not the king’s portrait,” they put him to death because he has insulted him. In particular, the authorities gather around it, honoring pieces of wood and paints because they fear the king.

If, then, these things happen to a portrait that has no spirit in it and does not move, being noncomposite, how much more to a human being, in whom God’s Spirit is at work, and who is honored above all the living creatures on earth!

But as for the various illnesses, colors, and weaknesses within us, they are [?] for us for the sake of our salvation. For none of these can diminish the glory God has given us, as Paul says, “For a man ought not to cover his head.”
When the blessed archbishop heard these words, he stood up and bowed down upon his neck, saying, “Truly, teaching should be entrusted to those who live alone in solitude.”
“For the thoughts of our hearts have entangled us, so that we have gone astray in all this way through ignorance.”
And immediately he sent a written message throughout the whole country, repudiating that statement: “It is mistaken, and we conceived it in foolishness.”
After this he adjured the blessed man, saying, “Tell me what your way of life is, and where you come from by birth. For I see that your appearance is like that of uneducated people.”
“Yet I hear your words, which are far more lofty than those of the wise.”
He answered, saying, “I have indeed wished to live as a monk, but I am far from that honor.”
“And I am also a man from Oxyrhynchus.”
“But because you are firmly grounded in your wisdom, the enemy set about doing this through you, knowing that many would take offense
because of this and suffer harm by not listening to the word of holy instruction that comes from your mouth.

Yet because of the love for God that is in you, you have overcome every kind of trick of the devil by listening to the words of my lowly self. For the greatness within you could not lift you up into a proud frame of mind and make you cling to your own will.

Instead, you displayed the humility that is in Christ, just as the great Moses himself listened to Jethro, the priest of Midian. This is truly what the Savior said to our fathers the apostles: ‘Humble yourselves and become like little children.’”
“But you have truly shown yourself, because you have turned entirely away from pride toward purity and the simplicity of lowliness.” After this he begged him to stay with him for some days.
But he pleaded, saying, “This is impossible for me.” And so he departed from him in peace and honor.
He was grieved at heart as he departed from him, like a child whose father is leaving him. Three years after these things happened, the bishop of Oxyrhynchus fell asleep.
And, according to custom, the whole city gathered together in unanimous agreement.
They voted for one of the priests, who was himself devout, and sent him to Alexandria with the resolutions so that they might make him bishop.
When the archbishop, Apa Theophilus, received the letters—

He answered, saying, “Aphou is a monk who belongs to your city. Bring him to me so that I may give him to you as bishop.” But the priests answered, saying, “We do not know of a monk named Aphou in our district, and we also think that none of us knows him.”
The archbishop answered them again, saying, “If you do not bring him to me, I will not appoint anyone for you now.”
They departed from him and went to their city.
They searched for the man, but no one knew him throughout the whole district.
For he was not living among people, but among wild animals.
When they became distressed, they gathered the monks together and questioned them about the man.
The one among them who knew him answered, “Yes, I have known him before today. I used to find him in the wilderness, grazing with the antelopes.”
They immediately ordered the hunters to set a trap for him and capture him, because the brother had told them, “If he learns that you are looking for him to make him a bishop, he will run away.”
So the hunters set their traps for him, and he came out that night to drink water with the antelopes.
Immediately the hunters sprang upon him, caught him, and held him.
He said to them, “What business do you have with me, that you are holding me? I too am a human being like you.”
“If you are catching animals, here is the antelope you have caught.”
They said to him, “We know that you are a human being, and we are looking for you. That is why we caught you.”
He said to them, “Then I am the one you are looking for. Leave this one alone; let it go.”
They immediately released the antelope, put him on a mount at once, and brought him to Alexandria before the archbishop.

When he saw him, he was very glad. When they told him how they had caught him, he was greatly astonished and said, “You have come, Aphou. Come, you too, and endure hardship with your fellow members. Until today you have struggled for yourself alone, saving yourself. Now, in turn, turn back and strengthen your brothers, and struggle for them as well as for yourself.”

Father Aphou answered, “Who am I, my lord and master, that you should say such things to me? I am a weak man, and because of my weakness I fled from association with people, so that I would not be swept away in the confusion of the waves of this life. Now I implore you by the Lord not to take me by force, for this task is beyond my strength.”
The archbishop was deeply distressed because of the oath by the Lord.

And he said to him, “As the Lord lives, if you do not release me from the oath with which you have bound me, I will make you a stranger to the entire calling of Christians, by the Lord [?], in this age and the one to come.”
Immediately Father Aphou bowed down, saying, “I have made my choice, for this is a danger to me and an affliction forever.
Look, I am at your disposal. If I can do the work, do with me as you wish.”
Immediately he bowed down and said, “Forgive me, my lord and father.”
He instructed him and sent him to his city. When he began his service as bishop, he also began another ascetic practice of this kind.
For throughout his entire episcopate, he did not spend a single night sleeping in the city, nor did he eat a single loaf of bread in it, even for a single day.

Instead, he ate alone in a monastery outside the city. On Saturday he would come to the church, gather the people, and speak to them about the word of God until evening. They would spend Saturday night holding their services, offering their prayers, and singing their psalms, while he stood over them during the holy liturgies.
He would also instruct them until the sixth hour on Sunday, and then withdraw again to his monastery until Saturday.
He appointed the priest whom they had brought to make bishop to oversee all the church’s accounting.

He would render the church’s accounts once a year, and everything left over after the church’s expenses he would distribute to the poor of the city and those nearby, so that through him they would forget the hardship of their poverty.
Indeed, other officials also contributed to him, apart from the church’s resources.
They would give him votive offerings and gifts.
He would distribute them to everyone according to each person’s need.
He would spend Saturday in [?]. He would attend to the needs of those who were in want and those who suffered injustice.

He would continue standing up for their appeals until the ninth hour. From the ninth hour onward, he would devote himself to holy prayer until evening. Then he would gather them and come out [?] again, and persevere in the night vigil until morning. No woman dared approach him to receive while wearing any gold.
This is how he gave orders that no woman should approach him to receive the body and blood of Christ while wearing any visible gold or any brightly colored clothing, because the deacons feared him.
They stood in order at each doorway, allowing no one to enter except those clothed in modesty.
That is, their faces and hands were covered, and the other garments they wore were not made of an embroiderer’s woven work.
And their complexion and appearance were also radiant.

The deacons likewise followed his example. None of them did anything unjust, nor did they charge interest. And not only he, but many others also gave up charging interest, striving to practice the way of life that leads to life.
The women also strove for sobriety, and none of them neglected service in the holy places.
As a result, throughout the whole city in those days people said, “These truly are the Lord’s people.”
For he often said to them during instruction, “My heart does not grieve for those who have been wronged as it does for those who wrong others.
For those who have been wronged reap for themselves a harvest from the kingdom of heaven.
But those who wrong others cut themselves off from it and reap for themselves a harvest of destruction.”
It also frequently happened that he would [?], and they would tell him about what was happening in the city.
And he would instruct the people to repent and keep wrath from overtaking them.
Even if the person singing the psalms omitted a word or changed it, he would forbid giving anything until the singer recited the words and corrected the psalm.
And he would say through his tears, “These words belong to a king. He spoke them with fasting and sackcloth.
But we shamelessly pay no attention to them.”

And when he was coming to the end of his life, the brothers approached him as he was about to die. Confident in the upright conduct of his people and the purity of his episcopal ministry, to which they bore witness, they said to him, “Our father, speak a word to us before you leave us.”
He spoke to them, saying, “There is just one thing I command you: none of you is to desire any position of greatness.
For even after I fled from it, I was barely able to preserve what I had gained in the monastic life.
As for being a bishop, I do not think I have gained anything from it in any respect. Indeed, I was barely able to preserve myself as I was before.”
And whenever he intended to appoint a deacon, he would not ordain him unless he first memorized twenty-five psalms, two letters of the apostle, and a portion of a Gospel.
But if he was to be a priest, he had to memorize a portion of Deuteronomy, a portion of Proverbs, and another portion of Isaiah.

And because of the rule he maintained, not many people entered work of this kind unless they first prepared themselves with complete steadfastness. Nor did it ever happen in his days that anyone took money for an ordination.

Rather, whenever someone was chosen from among the people for a position where he was needed, he would first have them remain patiently and demonstrate that they loved the word of God, so that they too would build up the people with this kind of perseverance. And this is how he brought his life to a good conclusion, going into God’s presence in peace on the twenty-first of Thoth, in Christ Jesus our Lord. Through him, glory belongs to God the Father, together with him and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.
